content: Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a frequent complication following diagnostic, therapeutic, or accidental lumbar punctures. Various pharmacological interventions have been employed in clinical practice to prevent PDPH, and some have been evaluated in clinical trials. However, uncertainties remain regarding their clinical efficacy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of drugs used to prevent PDPH in both adults and children. The search strategy included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies up to mid-2012. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing any drug for PDPH prevention were included, with no restrictions on language. A total of 10 RCTs involving 1611 participants were included in the review. The majority of participants were women (72%), with 913 being parturients undergoing lumbar puncture for regional anesthesia. The drugs evaluated included epidural and spinal morphine, spinal fentanyl, oral caffeine, rectal indomethacin, intravenous cosyntropin, intravenous aminophylline, and intravenous dexamethasone. All studies reported on the primary outcome, which was the incidence of PDPH of any severity following lumbar puncture. Epidural morphine and intravenous cosyntropin were found to reduce the incidence of PDPH of any severity when compared to placebo. Similarly, intravenous aminophylline reduced the incidence of PDPH when compared to no intervention. However, intravenous dexamethasone was associated with an increased incidence of PDPH. Adverse effects were noted with some interventions. Spinal morphine was associated with an increased incidence of pruritus compared to placebo, while epidural morphine increased the incidence of nausea and vomiting. Oral caffeine was linked to a higher incidence of insomnia compared to placebo. Other interventions, such as spinal fentanyl, rectal indomethacin, and intravenous dexamethasone, did not demonstrate significant effects on PDPH prevention or other outcomes. None of the included studies reported on the duration of hospital stay for patients. In conclusion, morphine (both epidural and spinal) and cosyntropin appear to be effective in reducing the incidence of PDPH, particularly in high-risk populations such as obstetric patients with inadvertent dural punctures. Aminophylline also showed efficacy in reducing PDPH in patients undergoing elective cesarean sections. However, dexamethasone was associated with an increased risk of PDPH following spinal anesthesia for cesarean sections. Morphine use was also linked to adverse effects, including pruritus, nausea, and vomiting. There is insufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy of other drugs, such as fentanyl, caffeine, indomethacin, and dexamethasone. These findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the limited data, potential biases, and small sample sizes of the included studies.
